title: 36k enemies repathing instantly (almost)
author: Such--Balance
selftext:
So i just used codex to migrate both pathfinding algorithms and enemy movement to c++ from in engine Godot.

massive improvement in functionality in both possible map sizes and total enemy numbers. Im pretty sure its still highly unoptimized and can probably be improved another 10x in efficiency.

Ive never used c++ so i was somewhat reluctant to migrate stuff to it. Would recommend though. Its just vastly more efficient for lost of stuff, and now in the days of ai doing the grunt work this really doesnt need all that much human effort to incorporate.

Heres some gains:

|Enemies|GDScript/update|Native/update|Speedup|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|500|1.64 ms|0.092 ms|17.7×|
|1,500|4.77 ms|0.208 ms|22.9×|
|3,000|9.76 ms|0.387 ms|25.2×|
|5,000|15.50 ms|0.622 ms|24.9×|

Measured accumulated CPU per completed wave, corridor maps, release build:

|Map|GDScript|Native|Speedup|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|100×100|91.0 ms|12.0 ms|7.6×|
|200×200|379.0 ms|47.1 ms|8.1×|
|512×512|2491.9 ms|313.9 ms|7.9×|

Absolutely disgusting. 

Keep in mind, im just a bag of meat with very little coding background and no pathfinding algorithm or optimization background whatsoever.

Im sure its possible to optimize it 10x more eventually with some finetuning. 

Im trying to build a few base pathfinding layers which should enable +- 500 active enemies on the map to path correctly, update asap to new or blocked of paths, and react to various layers in real time based off their 8 directional neighbors. 

This is the first layer which just points to the most optimal path. As my game eventually will have a lot off (breakable) walls, lots of fast and on the fly repathing is bound to happen and really this ground layer needs to both be dirt cheap compute wise, and update enemy pathing lighting fast.

36k is just a stress test as ill never gonna reach those numbers ingame. Any help is more than appreciated to if you have any tips or tricks or know some vids on this topic please let me know.

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: Those update times are impressive. Are you measuring the full frame too, including sending positions back to Godot and drawing 36k enemies? I'd also run the same scene with walls breaking every few seconds. That would show whether repathing remains cheap when the map changes during play.

replies.author: Such--Balance
replies.body:
Thanks!

Yeah its including those as this still runs via Godot itself.

Got a vid (although smaller and with less enemies) showing it with various walls opening and closing and how it updates and how it choses what to update first.

Its pretty nifty. Actually the first time i felt like i discovered something actually usefull myself. Although im sure im reinventing the wheel regardless.

Ill post it tomorrow and reply you the link here. But in short its 3 layers working together. One is the basic reupdating of the flow field. But before that theres an algoritm that tracks the actual wall surface thats being closed or opened, and if it encounters enemy paths, it also tracks that, as enemies 'mark' tiles they walk on.

Basically its using actual enemy pathing to optimize future pathfinding routes. Because in most cases, reapplying a flowfield only matters to <1% of all tiles, which happen to be tiles around walls and where enemies have or are currently walking anyways.

So it does that first in a split second, and after it updates the regular flowfield. Which leads to instant repathing, although not to perfect shortest routes, before the general flowfield takes over again

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
36k enemies repathing that quickly is impressive. At this point I would pay very close attention to how the data is laid out in memory, because the calculations themselves are usually the easy part. The CPU can do math incredibly quickly. A lot of the time it is waiting for the data it needs to arrive from memory.

For something like this, I would try to make the grid and enemies mostly indices into flat arrays:

    cost[cell]
    flowDirection[cell]
    blocked[cell]
    
    enemyCell[enemyIndex]
    enemyPosition[enemyIndex]

Now the CPU can process large chunks of related data sequentially. When it requests one value from memory, the surrounding values are likely pulled into the cache with it, so the next iterations of the loop can use data that is already close to the CPU instead of constantly jumping around memory.

I would also look at whether every wall change really requires recalculating the entire field. If you already know which cells changed, keep their indices and process those cells directly. The same applies to enemies. If only some enemies need to react to a change, keep those enemy indices rather than looping over all 36k and checking which ones need work.

That is one of the main ideas behind Data Oriented Design. Instead of making code faster, first organize the data so the CPU has less work to do and can access the data it needs efficiently.

I made a free Data Oriented Design skill for coding agents that covers a lot of these rules, which might be useful since you are doing this with Codex:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design* goes into CPU cache behavior, arrays, indices, branching, and reorganizing data to avoid unnecessary work. Most of those ideas are not specific to Unity.

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)
